chunks: "Inductive flyback, or inductive kick, is the voltage spike you get when you suddenly interrupt current through an inductor.

An inductor's voltage is L di over dt , so if I open a switch and the current tries to drop to zero in nanoseconds, the inductor generates a big voltage, with whatever polarity it needs, to keep the current flowing.
The energy 1 over 2 LI squared has to go somewhere.
If there's no path, it charges the stray capacitance of the switch and wiring, and the voltage can reach kilovolts, which blows up a transistor or arcs a relay contact.
It's unwanted when I'm driving a relay, a motor or a solenoid from a transistor or microcontroller pin.
The usual fix is a flyback or freewheel diode across the coil, reverse-biased in normal operation, so when the switch opens the current circulates through the diode and decays safely.
If I need faster release, I use a diode in series with a Zener or a TVS, which allows a higher clamp voltage and a faster decay, or an RC snubber.
A boost converter and a flyback converter deliberately interrupt inductor current so that the inductor's voltage adds to the input and steps the voltage up.
Ignition coils and camera flash circuits work the same way. So it's the same physics: in one case I clamp it, in the other I use it."
